posts.title_en: The carver had the last word
posts.summary_en: Around 1035 more than one runestone in four ended with a prayer to God. Fifty years later more of them ended with the carver's own name. But the signature did not push the prayer aside, and it did not follow demand – it followed the carvers. We think it spread as a custom from master to apprentice.
posts.body_en:
*Viðhugsi had this stone raised in memory of his good father. He lived in Ågersta. Here the stone shall stand between the farms. May the man who is skilled in runes interpret the runes that Balli carved.*

So it reads on a runestone at Ågersta in Uppland, carved some time between 1050 and 1080 to judge by its ornament. The father's name can be interpreted in two ways, but there is no doubt about the carver: Balli puts his name last, after a challenge to anyone who can read. He was not alone. On the earliest runestones the carver is almost never named, but on the last ones the carver's name stands on more than one stone in three, and nearly always at the very end. The last word, which a generation earlier was often a prayer to God, became the carver's.

![The runestone U 729](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/U729_%C3%85gersta_-_kmb.16000300012933.jpg/1280px-U729_%C3%85gersta_-_kmb.16000300012933.jpg)
U 729 at Ågersta in Uppland, carved by Balli. The text ends with *the runes that Balli carved*. Photo: Bengt A. Lundberg, [CC BY 2.5 SE](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5/se/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U729_%C3%85gersta_-_kmb.16000300012933.jpg).

:::box In short
- The carver's name – the signature – stands on 3 % of the earliest runestones and on 38 % of the last ones, nearly always at the end of the text.
- Around 1035 more texts ended with a prayer than with the carver's name. Fifty years later it was the other way round: the last word had passed from God to the carver.
- But the signature did not push the prayer off the stones, and it was not more common where many stones were raised. It followed the carvers: some signed one stone in three, others almost never.
- Our hypothesis: the signature spread as a custom among the carvers, from master to apprentice, not in answer to the patrons' demand. It can be tested.
:::

## The last word changes hands

We went through the 1,292 runestones in Sweden that have a legible text in the Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base. On 182 of them the carver wrote his name, with a carver's formula such as *Balli risti*, Balli carved. Nine signatures in ten stand among the last five words of the text. The prayer – *God help his soul* – usually comes last as well. And on the 36 stones that have both a prayer and a signature, the signature comes after the prayer, on every single one. The carver has the last word, after God.

So we can follow how the texts end. 740 of the dated stones have a surviving ending.

:::chart How the text ends, by style group
# With a prayer
RAK, around 1000 | 10 | 155 stones
Fp, around 1030 | 23 | 137 stones
Pr1, around 1030 | 19 | 47 stones
+Pr2, around 1035 | 27 | 81 stones
Pr3, around 1065 | 22 | 111 stones
Pr4, around 1085 | 7 | 180 stones
Pr5, around 1115 | 3 | 29 stones
# With the carver's name
RAK, around 1000 | 2 | 155 stones
Fp, around 1030 | 7 | 137 stones
Pr1, around 1030 | 13 | 47 stones
Pr2, around 1035 | 12 | 81 stones
Pr3, around 1065 | 22 | 111 stones
+Pr4, around 1085 | 22 | 180 stones
+Pr5, around 1115 | 38 | 29 stones
Source: Vitki's corpus analysis of the Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base; stones whose ending survives, dated by their style group (Gräslund 2006).
:::

Around 1035, in the style group Pr2, 27 % of the texts end with a prayer and 12 % with the carver's name. A generation later, in Pr3, they are equally common, 22 % each. In Pr4, around 1085, the balance has turned: 7 % end with a prayer and 22 % with the carver's name. Among the last runestones, in Pr5, 38 % end with the carver's name and 3 % with a prayer.

## The signature spreads

Counting all dated stones, not only those with a surviving ending, the carver's name stands on 3 % of the earliest (RAK) and on 38 % of the last (Pr5).

:::chart Share of runestones with the carver's name, by style group
+RAK, around 1000 | 3 | 169 stones
Fp, around 1030 | 7 | 149 stones
Pr1, around 1030 | 16 | 51 stones
Pr2, around 1035 | 13 | 87 stones
Pr3, around 1065 | 23 | 118 stones
Pr4, around 1085 | 23 | 198 stones
+Pr5, around 1115 | 38 | 32 stones
Source: as above, all dated stones with a legible text.
:::

Our model compares stones by the same carver and in the same area. With it the share rises from about 6 per cent around the year 1000 to 28 per cent in the early 1100s – an increase of 22 percentage points, probably somewhere between 10 and 36.

The last bar needs an explanation. 28 of the 32 stones in Pr5 were carved by one and the same carver, Œpir, who signed about one stone in three that he made. That bar is therefore largely his. But the increase is not down to him: without Œpir's stones the share rises from 3 % in RAK to 23 % in Pr3 and 19 % in Pr4.

![The runestone U 104](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/U_104%2C_Ed.jpg/1280px-U_104%2C_Ed.jpg)
U 104 at Ed church in Uppland, one of Œpir's stones. The text ends *ØpiR risti*, Œpir carved. Photo: Berig, [CC BY 2.5](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U_104,_Ed.jpg).

:::box How sure we are
A pattern in a large material can arise by chance, or because the material is skewed. So we have tested it in several ways:

- **Same carver, same area.** The model compares stones by the same carver and in the same area. The increase is therefore not just a difference between carvers or between provinces.
- **Many tests at once.** We tested 14 features at the same time and adjusted for it (Holm's method). The rise of the signature survives the adjustment (adjusted p 0.002): a pattern this clear would arise by chance among the 14 features in fewer than one case in 500.
- **Two independent halves.** We split the stones into two groups, parish by parish, so that both groups got stones from the same districts and about the same time, and redid the whole analysis in each group on its own. The pattern shows in both: from 7 to 28 % in one and from 1 to 24 % in the other. Had it been found in only one, it could have been down to a few particular parishes or carvers.
- **Uncertain years.** The style groups' dates are approximate. We recalculated ten times with years drawn at random within each group's interval, and all ten gave a clear increase, between 13 and 21 percentage points.
- **Our search and Rundata's.** We find signatures by searching for carver's formulas (*risti*, *hiogg*, *markaði* …) and may miss rare forms. Rundata's own record of which stones are signed gives the same picture: from 4 % in RAK to 38 % in Pr5.
:::

## Our hypothesis – and two tests

That carvers sign more and more often is known, especially in Uppland, and Magnus Källström has studied the signatures thoroughly (2007). What we add is the measurement with carver and area held constant, and the observation that the signature takes over the last place in the text just as the prayer leaves it. That calls for an explanation.

The nearest explanation is that rune carving became a trade: carvers with many commissions put their name on the work, as a master's mark – perhaps as advertising. That explanation has two consequences that can be tested.

**Did the signature push the prayer aside?** If the carver's name replaced the prayer as the ending of the text, a stone with a prayer should rarely have a signature – they would compete for the same place. We compared stones within the same style group (804 dated stones). A stone with a prayer was signed just as often as a stone without one from the same time. The odds ratio is 1.1, in practice no difference, and it probably lies between 0.6 and 1.9 (p 0.69: a difference of that size easily arises by chance). The prayer and the signature were chosen separately. The last word changed hands because prayers became fewer and signatures more frequent, not because one pushed the other aside.

**Did the signature follow demand?** If the signature was a master's advertisement, it should be most common where many stones were raised, for there were the most patrons and the most carvers to compete with. We counted how many runestones stand within ten kilometres of each stone and split the stones into three equal groups, from the sparsest districts (at most 22 stones within ten kilometres) to the densest (more than 55). In the later style groups, Pr3 to Pr5, when the signature was common, the share of signed stones is almost the same in all three: 25, 24 and 24 %. In a model with style group and province there is no association (p 0.29). The signature was not more common where the market was largest.

**It followed the carvers.** What makes the difference is the carver. Œpir put his name on 38 % of the stones we can read, Balli on 37 % and Ásmundr on 27 %. Fótr, who was active at the same time and also has many stones, signed 10 %, and Gunnarr, one of the early carvers, 3 %. Having many commissions did not by itself lead to a signature. It was something some carvers did and others did not.

So we state the hypothesis more sharply:

> The signature spread as a custom among the carvers – from master to apprentice and between carvers who worked side by side – not in answer to the patrons' demand.

The tests have their limits: the number of stones within ten kilometres is a rough measure of demand, and the style groups divide time into steps of about twenty-five years.

## How the hypothesis can be tested further

1. **The carvers' network.** If the signature was passed on between carvers, carvers who worked together or learnt from each other should sign about equally often, wherever they worked.
2. **The words of the signature.** The formulas vary – *risti*, *hiogg*, *markaði* – and sometimes praise follows, as in Balli's challenge to the rune-skilled. If a custom spread, the wording should follow the carvers' schools rather than the provinces.
3. **The carver's own career.** If signing was something a carver learnt or grew into, the share of signed stones may rise within one carver's career. That requires each carver's stones to be dated more finely than the style groups allow.
4. **The costly stones.** If the signature was a selling point after all, it should be more common on the largest and most elaborate stones. The stones' measurements exist for part of the material.

## Caveats

- The dating rests on the ornament and is approximate, and the style groups were worked out for the stones of Uppland and Södermanland.
- Signatures are found by searching for carver's formulas in Rundata's normalised text, and a damaged text can hide a signature. So we follow the ending of the text only on stones whose ending survives.
- Many carvers are known precisely through their signatures, and unsigned stones have been attributed to them by style. The share of signed stones per carver therefore rests on the scholars' attributions.
- The last style group, Pr5, consists largely of Œpir's stones.
- An association in time is not a cause. The hypothesis explains the pattern, but other explanations are possible – for example that more people could read, so that a name on the stone found more readers.

posts.title: Bönen tystnade – men korset stod kvar
posts.summary: Omkring år 1035 bad mer än var tredje runsten Gud om hjälp för den dödes själ. Femtio år senare gjorde bara en av tio det, fast korset fanns kvar på stenarna. Vi tror att bönen inte försvann – den flyttade in i kyrkan.
posts.body:
*Tova och Häming lät resa denna sten efter Gunnar, sin son. Han dog ute bland grekerna. Gud hjälpe hans själ och Guds moder.*

Så står det på en runsten vid Åshusby i Uppland, ristad någon gång mellan 1020 och 1050 att döma av ornamentiken och tillskriven ristaren Åsmund. Den sista meningen är en bön, och den är inte ovanlig: ungefär var femte runsten med läsbar text ber Gud, Kristus eller Guds moder att hjälpa den döde. Men när vi följde bönen genom tiden såg vi något som förvånade oss. Bönen kommer och går – medan korset stannar.

![Runstenen U 431](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/U_431%2C_%C3%85shusby.JPG/1280px-U_431%2C_%C3%85shusby.JPG)
U 431 vid Åshusby i Uppland. Bönen – *Gud hjälpe hans själ och Guds moder* – står sist i texten. Foto: Berig, [CC BY 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U_431,_%C3%85shusby.JPG).

:::box Kort sagt
- Kristna böner på runstenar var vanligast under 1030- och 1040-talen och nästan borta i början av 1100-talet.
- Korset finns kvar på en stor del av stenarna, omkring sex av tio i de sena stilgrupperna. Det var inte kristendomen som försvann, utan bönen.
- Samtidigt blir det allt vanligare att ristaren skriver sitt namn på stenen.
- Vår hypotes: bönen tystnade när förbönen för de döda blev kyrkans sak. Den kan prövas.
:::

## Bönen kommer – och går

Vi gick igenom de 1 292 runstenar i Sverige som har en läsbar text i Samnordisk runtextdatabas och letade efter böner: *Gud hjälpe hans själ*, *Gud hjälpe hans ande*, *Guds moder* och deras många stavningar. 804 av stenarna kan dateras ungefär genom sin ornamentik. Runstenskonsten bytte stil under 1000-talet, och forskarna har ordnat stilarna i en följd, från RAK omkring år 1000 till Pr5 i början av 1100-talet.

:::chart Andel runstenar med kristen bön, efter stilgrupp
RAK, omkring 1000 | 15 | 169 stenar
Fp, omkring 1030 | 28 | 149 stenar
Pr1, omkring 1030 | 24 | 51 stenar
+Pr2, omkring 1035 | 37 | 87 stenar
Pr3, omkring 1065 | 29 | 118 stenar
Pr4, omkring 1085 | 10 | 198 stenar
Pr5, omkring 1115 | 3 | 32 stenar
Källa: Vitkis korpusanalys av Samnordisk runtextdatabas; stenarna är daterade efter sin stilgrupp (Gräslund 2006).
:::

Bönen blir vanligare under 1000-talets första hälft och når sin topp med stilgruppen Pr2, omkring 1035, då 37 % av stenarna bär en bön. Sedan faller den brant: 10 % i Pr4 och 3 % i Pr5, bland de sista runstenarna. Vår modell, som tar hänsyn till vem som ristade stenen och var den står, lägger toppen omkring 1038 (mellan 1023 och 1048) och visar en nedgång från omkring 30 till 2 procent i början av 1100-talet.

## Det var inte tron som försvann

Man kunde tro att bönen försvinner för att stenarna blir mindre kristna. Korset talar emot det. Det finns på 46 % av de tidigaste stenarna, på 70 % omkring 1035 och fortfarande på 62 % i Pr4 och Pr5, långt efter att bönen har börjat tystna. Med samma modell som för bönen minskar visserligen också korset efter toppen omkring 1028, från omkring 70 till 40 procent, men den minskningen håller inte i båda halvorna av materialet. Bönen faller till en femtondel; korset finns kvar på en stor del av stenarna. Det är bönen, uppmaningen till Gud att hjälpa den döde, som nästan försvinner.

:::chart Korset och ristarens namn på samma stenar
# Kors
RAK, omkring 1000 | 46 | 169 stenar
Fp, omkring 1030 | 68 | 149 stenar
Pr1, omkring 1030 | 76 | 51 stenar
Pr2, omkring 1035 | 70 | 87 stenar
Pr3, omkring 1065 | 63 | 118 stenar
+Pr4, omkring 1085 | 62 | 198 stenar
+Pr5, omkring 1115 | 62 | 32 stenar
# Ristarens signatur
RAK, omkring 1000 | 3 | 169 stenar
Fp, omkring 1030 | 7 | 149 stenar
Pr1, omkring 1030 | 16 | 51 stenar
Pr2, omkring 1035 | 13 | 87 stenar
Pr3, omkring 1065 | 23 | 118 stenar
+Pr4, omkring 1085 | 23 | 198 stenar
+Pr5, omkring 1115 | 38 | 32 stenar
Källa: som ovan.
:::

Samtidigt händer något annat: ristarna börjar signera. På de tidigaste stenarna står ristarens namn på 3 %, på de sista på 38 %. *Öpir ristade*, står det på stenen vid Morby i Uppland, där en mor lät bygga en bro för sin dotters själ – utan en bön.

![Runstenen U 489](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/U_489%2C_Morby.jpg/1280px-U_489%2C_Morby.jpg)
U 489 vid Morby i Uppland, ristad av Öpir under stilgruppen Pr4: en bro för en dotters själ, ristarens namn – men ingen bön. Foto: Christine Jewell from Canada, [CC BY-SA 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U_489,_Morby.jpg).

:::box Så säkra är vi
Ett mönster i ett stort material kan uppstå av en slump, eller av att materialet är skevt. Därför har vi prövat det på flera sätt:

- **Samma ristare, samma trakt.** Modellen jämför stenar som har ristats av samma ristare och står i samma område. Nedgången är alltså inte bara en enskild ristares vana eller en skillnad mellan landskap.
- **Många test på en gång.** Vi prövade 14 drag samtidigt och justerade för det (Holms metod). Bönens förändring klarar justeringen med god marginal (justerat p under 0,001): ett så tydligt mönster skulle uppstå av en slump bland de 14 dragen i mindre än ett fall på tusen.
- **Två oberoende halvor.** Vi delade stenarna i två grupper, socken för socken, så att båda grupperna fick stenar från samma trakter och ungefär samma tid, och gjorde om hela analysen i varje grupp för sig. Mönstret syns i båda. Hade det bara funnits i den ena hade det kunnat bero på några enskilda socknar eller ristare.
- **Osäkra årtal.** Stilgruppernas dateringar är ungefärliga. Vi räknade om tio gånger med årtal lottade inom varje stilgrupps intervall, och alla tio gav samma resultat.
- **Skadade stenar.** Bönen står oftast sist i texten, där många stenar är skadade. Med bara de stenar vars slut är bevarat består nedgången.
- **Vår egen sökning.** Inför inlägget kontrollerade vi sökningen efter böner och hittade stavningar den missade, som *hiælpi* och *hialpin*. Siffrorna här bygger på den rättade sökningen.
:::

## Vår hypotes: bönen flyttade in i kyrkan

Att runstenar bär böner är välkänt, och forskningen har länge sett runstenarna som en del av kristnandet. Det vi tillför är mätningen: att bönens uppgång och fall går att följa med ristare och trakt konstanta, och att den skiljer sig från korset, som består. Det kräver en förklaring.

Vår hypotes är att bönen på stenen var lekfolkets egen förbön under missionstiden. Under 1000-talets första hälft fanns ännu få kyrkor och präster i Mälardalen. Den som ville att någon skulle be för den dödes själ kunde sätta bönen där den syntes – på stenen vid vägen, kanske i hopp om att förbipasserande skulle be. När kyrkan växte fram under 1000-talets andra hälft, med präster, vigd jord och mässor för de döda, blev förbönen kyrkans uppgift. Stenen behövde inte längre be. Den fortsatte att bära korset, som ett tecken för tron och släkten, och blev alltmer ett minnesmärke – signerat av sin ristare.

## En första prövning: ett skifte samtidigt överallt

Om det var den lokala kyrkan som gjorde stenens bön överflödig, borde bönen tystna tidigare där kyrkorna kom tidigt. Det kunde vi pröva. Vi tog de medeltida kyrkor i Wikidata som är uppförda senast år 1200 och jämförde stenar nära och långt från dem, bara stenar som står kvar på sin ursprungliga plats (504 daterade stenar).

Resultatet var tydligt, men inte det vi väntade oss. Bönen är något vanligare nära de tidiga kyrkorna, men den tystnar lika snabbt överallt: efter omkring 1075 bär 4 % av stenarna inom tre kilometer från en tidig kyrka en bön (25 stenar), och 3 % av dem längre bort (118 stenar). Vi ser inget tecken på att bönen försvann tidigare nära kyrkorna (p 0,28 för skillnaden i hur snabbt den försvinner).

Det talar emot den enklaste formen av hypotesen – att varje gård slutade be på sin sten när den fick sin kyrka – och för ett gemensamt skifte som slog igenom ungefär samtidigt i hela Mälardalen. Ett sådant skifte kunde komma uppifrån: under 1000-talets andra hälft började kyrkan organiseras i stift, och Sigtuna nämns som biskopssäte omkring 1060. Vi formulerar därför hypotesen skarpare:

> Bönen tystnade när förbönen för de döda blev en sak för den organiserade kyrkan, inte för den enskilda släkten.

Prövningen har en gräns: stilgrupperna delar in tiden i steg om ungefär tjugofem år, så en skillnad på något decennium skulle inte synas.

## Så kan hypotesen prövas vidare

1. **Finare datering.** Om ristarnas verksamhet dateras finare, genom ristarnas samarbeten och kedjor av lärare och elever, går det att se om bönen tystnar samtidigt överallt eller om skiftet sprider sig från stiftens centra.
2. **Bönens ord.** Om kyrkan tog över förbönen bör bönernas ordval närma sig kyrkans språk innan de försvinner. Guds moder nämns i 27 % av bönerna i Pr2 och 25 % i Pr3, mot 12 % i RAK och 5 % i Pr4 – ett spår att följa, även om antalet böner per stilgrupp är litet.
3. **Andra landskap och länder.** Där kyrkan organiserades tidigare eller senare bör bönen ha tystnat tidigare respektive senare. En jämförelse med Danmark kräver bättre uppgifter om korsen på de danska stenarna än vi har i dag.
4. **Gåvor för själen.** Om förbönen flyttade in i kyrkan kan gåvor för den dödes själ – till kyrkan eller i form av broar – ha tagit bönens plats. Brobyggen ökar inte tydligt i vårt material, och gåvor till kyrkan syns inte på stenarna; här behövs andra källor.

## Förbehåll

- Dateringen bygger på ornamentiken och är ungefärlig, och stilgrupperna är utarbetade för stenarna i Uppland och Södermanland.
- Böner hittas genom att söka i Rundatas normaliserade text. En skadad text kan dölja en bön; därför prövade vi stenar med bevarat slut för sig.
- Ett samband i tid är inte en orsak. Hypotesen förklarar mönstret, men andra förklaringar är möjliga – till exempel att en ny generation ristare hade andra ideal. Att mönstret håller med ristaren konstant talar dock emot att det bara är ett generationsskifte.
- Under arbetet hittade vi också ett fel i hur appen räknar bort stenar som har flyttats till kyrkor. Det påverkar inte huvudfyndet, som inte bygger på var stenarna står, men prövningen mot de tidiga kyrkorna är gjord med det rättade urvalet. Felet har rättats i appen och beskrivs i metodbeskrivningen.

posts.title_en: The prayer fell silent – but the cross remained
posts.summary_en: Around the year 1035 more than one runestone in three asked God to help the soul of the dead. Fifty years later only one in ten did, although the cross remained on the stones. We think the prayer did not disappear – it moved into the church.
posts.body_en:
*Tófa and Hemingr had this stone raised in memory of Gunnarr, their son. He died abroad among the Greeks. May God and God's mother help his soul.*

So reads a runestone at Åshusby in Uppland, carved some time between 1020 and 1050 to judge by its ornament and attributed to the carver Åsmundr. The last sentence is a prayer, and it is not unusual: about one in five runestones with a legible text asks God, Christ or God's mother to help the dead. But when we followed the prayer through time we saw something that surprised us. The prayer comes and goes – while the cross stays.

![The runestone U 431](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/U_431%2C_%C3%85shusby.JPG/1280px-U_431%2C_%C3%85shusby.JPG)
U 431 at Åshusby in Uppland. The prayer – *May God and God's mother help his soul* – comes last in the text. Photo: Berig, [CC BY 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U_431,_%C3%85shusby.JPG).

:::box In short
- Christian prayers on runestones were most common in the 1030s and 1040s and almost gone by the early 1100s.
- The cross remains on a large share of the stones, about six in ten in the late style groups. It was not Christianity that disappeared, but the prayer.
- At the same time it becomes ever more common for the carver to sign the stone.
- Our hypothesis: the prayer fell silent when intercession for the dead became the church's task. It can be tested.
:::

## The prayer comes – and goes

We went through the 1,292 runestones in Sweden that have a legible text in the Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base and looked for prayers: *God help his soul*, *God help his spirit*, *God's mother* and their many spellings. 804 of the stones can be roughly dated by their ornament. Runestone art changed style during the eleventh century, and scholars have put the styles in order, from RAK around the year 1000 to Pr5 in the early 1100s.

:::chart Share of runestones with a Christian prayer, by style group
RAK, around 1000 | 15 | 169 stones
Fp, around 1030 | 28 | 149 stones
Pr1, around 1030 | 24 | 51 stones
+Pr2, around 1035 | 37 | 87 stones
Pr3, around 1065 | 29 | 118 stones
Pr4, around 1085 | 10 | 198 stones
Pr5, around 1115 | 3 | 32 stones
Source: Vitki's corpus analysis of the Scandinavian Runic-text Data Base; stones dated by their style group (Gräslund 2006).
:::

The prayer becomes more common in the first half of the eleventh century and peaks with the style group Pr2, around 1035, when 37 % of the stones carry a prayer. Then it falls steeply: 10 % in Pr4 and 3 % in Pr5, among the last runestones. Our model, which takes into account who carved the stone and where it stands, puts the peak around 1038 (between 1023 and 1048) and shows a decline from about 30 to 2 per cent in the early 1100s.

## It was not the faith that disappeared

One might think that the prayer disappears because the stones become less Christian. The cross speaks against that. It is found on 46 % of the earliest stones, on 70 % around 1035 and still on 62 % in Pr4 and Pr5, long after the prayer has begun to fall silent. With the same model as for the prayer the cross does decline after its peak around 1028, from about 70 to 40 per cent, but that decline does not hold in both halves of the material. The prayer falls to a fifteenth; the cross remains on a large share of the stones. It is the prayer, the plea to God to help the dead, that almost disappears.

:::chart The cross and the carver's name on the same stones
# Cross
RAK, around 1000 | 46 | 169 stones
Fp, around 1030 | 68 | 149 stones
Pr1, around 1030 | 76 | 51 stones
Pr2, around 1035 | 70 | 87 stones
Pr3, around 1065 | 63 | 118 stones
+Pr4, around 1085 | 62 | 198 stones
+Pr5, around 1115 | 62 | 32 stones
# Carver's signature
RAK, around 1000 | 3 | 169 stones
Fp, around 1030 | 7 | 149 stones
Pr1, around 1030 | 16 | 51 stones
Pr2, around 1035 | 13 | 87 stones
Pr3, around 1065 | 23 | 118 stones
+Pr4, around 1085 | 23 | 198 stones
+Pr5, around 1115 | 38 | 32 stones
Source: as above.
:::

At the same time something else happens: the carvers begin to sign. The carver's name appears on 3 % of the earliest stones and on 38 % of the last. *Œpir carved*, says the stone at Morby in Uppland, where a mother had a bridge built for her daughter's soul – without a prayer.

![The runestone U 489](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/U_489%2C_Morby.jpg/1280px-U_489%2C_Morby.jpg)
U 489 at Morby in Uppland, carved by Œpir in style group Pr4: a bridge for a daughter's soul, the carver's name – but no prayer. Photo: Christine Jewell from Canada, [CC BY-SA 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U_489,_Morby.jpg).

:::box How sure we are
A pattern in a large material can arise by chance, or because the material is skewed. So we have tested it in several ways:

- **Same carver, same area.** The model compares stones carved by the same carver and standing in the same area. The decline is therefore not just one carver's habit or a difference between provinces.
- **Many tests at once.** We tested 14 features at the same time and adjusted for it (Holm's method). The change in the prayer passes the adjustment with a good margin (adjusted p below 0.001): a pattern this clear would arise by chance among the 14 features in fewer than one case in a thousand.
- **Two independent halves.** We split the stones into two groups, parish by parish, so that both groups got stones from the same districts and about the same time, and redid the whole analysis in each group on its own. The pattern appears in both. Had it been found in only one, it could have been down to a few particular parishes or carvers.
- **Uncertain years.** The style groups' dates are approximate. We recalculated ten times with years drawn at random within each style group's interval, and all ten gave the same result.
- **Damaged stones.** The prayer usually comes last in the text, where many stones are damaged. With only the stones whose end is preserved, the decline remains.
- **Our own search.** Before writing this post we checked the search for prayers and found spellings it missed, such as *hiælpi* and *hialpin*. The figures here use the corrected search.
:::

## Our hypothesis: the prayer moved into the church

That runestones carry prayers is well known, and scholars have long seen the runestones as part of the conversion. What we add is the measurement: the rise and fall of the prayer can be followed with carver and area held constant, and it differs from the cross, which remains. That calls for an explanation.

Our hypothesis is that the prayer on the stone was the laity's own intercession during the mission period. In the first half of the eleventh century there were still few churches and priests in the Mälaren valley. Whoever wanted someone to pray for the soul of the dead could put the prayer where it was seen – on the stone by the road, perhaps in the hope that passers-by would pray. When the church grew in the second half of the century, with priests, consecrated ground and masses for the dead, intercession became the church's task. The stone no longer needed to pray. It went on carrying the cross, as a sign of faith and family, and increasingly became a memorial – signed by its carver.

## A first test: a shift at the same time everywhere

If it was the local church that made the stone's prayer superfluous, the prayer should fall silent earlier where churches came early. That we could test. We took the medieval churches in Wikidata built by the year 1200 and compared stones near and far from them, using only stones still standing where they were raised (504 dated stones).

The result was clear, but not what we expected. The prayer is somewhat more common near the early churches, but it falls silent just as fast everywhere: after about 1075, 4 % of the stones within three kilometres of an early church carry a prayer (25 stones), and 3 % of those further away (118 stones). We see no sign that the prayer disappeared earlier near the churches (p 0.28 for the difference in how fast it disappears).

That speaks against the simplest form of the hypothesis – that each farm stopped praying on its stone when it got its church – and for a common shift that took hold at about the same time throughout the Mälaren valley. Such a shift could come from above: in the second half of the eleventh century the church began to be organised in dioceses, and Sigtuna is mentioned as a bishop's seat around 1060. We therefore state the hypothesis more sharply:

> The prayer fell silent when intercession for the dead became a matter for the organised church, not for the individual family.

The test has a limit: the style groups divide time into steps of about twenty-five years, so a difference of a decade or so would not show.

## How the hypothesis can be tested further

1. **Finer dating.** If the carvers' careers are dated more finely, through their collaborations and chains of masters and pupils, it can be seen whether the prayer falls silent at the same time everywhere or whether the shift spreads from the centres of the dioceses.
2. **The words of the prayer.** If the church took over intercession, the wording of the prayers should approach the church's language before they disappear. God's mother is named in 27 % of the prayers in Pr2 and 25 % in Pr3, against 12 % in RAK and 5 % in Pr4 – a lead to follow, even though the number of prayers per style group is small.
3. **Other provinces and countries.** Where the church was organised earlier or later, the prayer should have fallen silent earlier or later. A comparison with Denmark needs better records of the crosses on the Danish stones than we have today.
4. **Gifts for the soul.** If intercession moved into the church, gifts for the soul of the dead – to the church or as bridges – may have taken the prayer's place. Bridge building does not clearly increase in our material, and gifts to the church do not show on the stones; other sources are needed here.

## Caveats

- The dating rests on the ornament and is approximate, and the style groups were worked out for the stones of Uppland and Södermanland.
- Prayers are found by searching the normalised text in Rundata. A damaged text can hide a prayer; we therefore tested stones with a preserved end on their own.
- An association in time is not a cause. The hypothesis explains the pattern, but other explanations are possible – for example that a new generation of carvers had other ideals. That the pattern holds with the carver held constant speaks against it being merely a change of generation.
- While working on this we also found an error in how the app leaves out stones that have been moved to churches. It does not affect the main finding, which does not depend on where the stones stand, but the test against the early churches uses the corrected selection. The error has been fixed in the app and is described in the methods.
